4:3.text: Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.

provenance.other: “with joy, and not with” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 13:17. The Book of Mormon completes the phrase with 'sorrow' where the KJV has 'grief', and then adds a third term, 'neither with contempt', which is its own.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 13:17 is addressed to a congregation about its leaders: obey them, because they watch for your souls as men who must give account, so that they may do it 'with joy, and not with grief'. Jacob has opened this chapter as exactly such a man — 'I, Jacob, having ministered much unto my people' — and the thing he wants received with joy is the account he is engraving. Recover the source and the borrowed clause turns out to be about a minister's reckoning for the people he served, which is what the plates are: Jacob's account, and the joy or grief with which his readers will take it. The letter's second-person burden ('that they may do it') has been transposed into the writer's hope for a reader four hundred years off.

4:3.note: 'Hoping that our beloved brethren, and our children, will receive them with thankful hearts, and look upon them, that they may learn with joy, and not with sorrow, neither with contempt.' Four words of Hebrews 13:17 in order, from the only KJV verse that has them, and the substitution of 'sorrow' for 'grief' is the kind of near-synonym exchange that marks a phrase carried in memory rather than copied. The two triads also correspond: Hebrews sets joy against grief and calls the alternative 'unprofitable for you'; Jacob sets joy against sorrow and against contempt, contempt being what makes an inheritance unprofitable to an heir.

4:4.text: Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.

provenance.other: “the prophets which were before” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:12, where it ends 'before you'. Jacob 4:4 ends it 'before us'. The nearer synoptic parallel, Luke 6:23, reads 'so did their fathers unto the prophets' and does not have the phrase.
provenance.significance: The Beatitudes' last blessing is a blessing on a persecuted line: rejoice, because that is how they treated the prophets which were before you. Jacob takes the same five words and turns them from a consolation into a claim of company — the holy prophets before us also had a hope of his glory. The clause that in Matthew marks a succession of suffering marks in Jacob a succession of foreknowledge, and ten verses later, at 4:14, Jacob will supply the persecution Matthew's clause implies: the Jews 'killed the Prophets'.

4:4.note: 'And not only we, ourselves, had a hope of his glory, but also all the Holy Prophets which were before us.' The five-word run is a KJV singleton and the only change is the pronoun, which the sentence requires: Matthew's speaker addresses a persecuted 'you', Jacob's writes himself into the line as 'us'. The verse is well short of Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his quotations; it is catalogued here on rarity, not length. The 'hope of his glory', twice in this verse, is the KJV's 'the hope of glory' (Colossians 1:27, a singleton), which returns at 4:11 in fuller form and is adjudicated there.

4:5.text: Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.

provenance.mt: Genesis 15:6 — 'And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.'
provenance.route: Genesis 15:6 → Galatians 3:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV renders the Abraham formula four different ways. Genesis 15:6: 'he COUNTED it to him for righteousness'. Romans 4:3: 'it was COUNTED unto him for righteousness'. James 2:23: 'it was IMPUTED unto him for righteousness'. Galatians 3:6: 'it was ACCOUNTED to him for righteousness'. “accounted to him for righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Jacob 4:5 reads 'even as it was accounted unto Abraham'.
provenance.significance: A mediation case decided by one word, and the second in this chapter. Genesis 15:6 is quoted three times in the New Testament and the KJV translators gave it a different verb each time; the Book of Mormon has the verb of Galatians, not of Genesis, of Romans, or of James. Recover Galatians 3 and the argument around that verb is precisely Jacob's: whether the law is kept for its own sake or as a witness to Christ. Paul asks the Galatians whether they received the Spirit 'by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith' and then produces Abraham as the answer; Jacob says 'we keep the law of Moses, it pointing our souls to him', and produces Abraham as the same answer. The one word carries the whole chapter of Galatians behind it.
provenance.alternative: Hebrews 11:17-19, which also reads Abraham's obedience as faith, is the source of the second half of this verse (below) and would be available for the first half as well — but it does not contain the righteousness formula in any form.

4:5.note: 'It is sanctified unto us for righteousness, even as it was accounted unto Abraham … to be obedient unto the commands of God, in offering up his son Isaac.' `mediation-check.py` returns one decisive point here: 'was accounted' is Galatians 3:6's form and is in no other KJV verse. Note that the Book of Mormon has also moved the formula off Abraham's belief and onto his obedience — in all four biblical versions what is accounted for righteousness is that Abraham believed, whereas Jacob attaches it to the offering of Isaac, which is James 2:21-23's reading of the same verse fitted to Galatians' wording.

4:5.text: By faith Abraham, when he was tried, offered up Isaac: and he that had received the promises offered up his only begotten son,

provenance.other: “offered up his only begotten son” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:17, and it is the only place outside the Johannine writings where the KJV uses 'only begotten son' at all. Jacob 4:5 holds the offering of Isaac and 'his only begotten Son' in a single clause. Hardy's apparatus points Genesis 22:1-18 at this verse — the narrative itself, behind the Hebrews sentence that reports it. The reference was read as standing at Jacob 3:5 until the study edition's running heads were used to bound each page (2026-09-05); it belongs here, where Jacob names the offering of Isaac outright.
provenance.significance: In Hebrews the only begotten son IS Isaac; in Jacob the offering of Isaac is 'a similitude of God and his only begotten Son', so the title has slid from the type to the antitype while the sentence around it stays where Hebrews put it. That is the interesting move, and Frederick makes it: he observes that Hebrews 11:17 is the sole non-Johannine New Testament use of the title, that Jacob 4:4-5 uses it in the same setting of Abraham's sacrifice, and that the title 'has been switched from referring to Isaac in Hebrews 11:17 to referring to Jesus in Jacob 4:4-5'; on that basis, and because in his judgment Jacob echoes Paul more than John, he suggests the provenance of the verse is Hebrews rather than John. This catalogue reaches the same conclusion by a different route — the four-word run is a KJV singleton — and the agreement is worth something because the routes differ (CONVENTIONS §3a).
provenance.alternative: John 3:16 supplies 'his only begotten Son' with a giving Father and is the more familiar home of the phrase; Frederick's own note weighs and sets it aside for this verse.

4:5.note: 'In offering up his son Isaac, which was a similitude of God and his only begotten Son.' Hebrews 11:17 is the one KJV verse that puts the offering and the title together, and Jacob 4:5 is the one Book of Mormon verse that does. Frederick discusses Jacob 4:4-5 at length in a note on the Book of Mormon's use of 'Only Begotten Son' and argues for Hebrews over John here; he is not compiling an index of sources, so the observation is an argument about a title, not a citation entry, but it is a real attribution and it is on this verse. Note also 1 Nephi's route through Hebrews 11 in order (11:8, 11:9, 11:13, 11:29 across 1 Nephi 2-5): the chapter of Hebrews that supplied Lehi's departure supplies Jacob's Isaac.

4:5.text: But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him.

provenance.other: “worship the Father in” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 4:23, where the phrase completes as 'in spirit and in truth'. Jacob 4:5 completes it twice as 'in his name'. Frederick, discussing the clauses of D&C 20:29, notes that the phrase 'worship the Father in his name' is not found in John and locates it in only two places, 2 Nephi 25:16 and this verse.
provenance.significance: Whatever the route, the substitution is doctrinally the point of the verse: John's true worshippers are marked off by the manner of their worship, Jacob's by its name. He is arguing that pre-Christian Nephites are Christians, and the qualifier that does the work is the one he has changed.

4:5.whyNot: Only the four common words are shared, and each of them is common; the distinctive half of John's clause ('in spirit and in truth') is absent, and the distinctive half of Jacob's ('in his name') is absent from John. Frederick's observation that the full Book of Mormon phrase is not biblical cuts against a direct borrowing. The rarity count is real but four such words can co-occur by construction.
4:5.note: 'They believed in Christ, and worshiped the Father in his name; and also, we worship the Father in his name.' Recorded at moderate because the four-word sequence is a KJV singleton and because John 4 is the KJV's one sustained discussion of how the Father is to be worshipped, which is what this verse is doing; declined above moderate because the phrase that Jacob actually repeats twice is not a biblical phrase at all.

4:6.text: And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

provenance.other: “the spirit of prophecy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 19:10: 'for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy'.
provenance.significance: Jacob's list is 'we search the Prophets; and we have many revelations, and the spirit of prophecy; and having all these witnesses'. Revelation 19:10 is the verse that defines the borrowed term, and defines it as a testimony — 'the testimony of Jesus IS the spirit of prophecy' — which is exactly the use Jacob puts it to when he calls the three items witnesses. The definition travels with the phrase.

4:6.note: A KJV singleton, and the sense comes with it. The angel's refusal in Revelation 19:10 is also the scene 1 Nephi 17:55 borrowed for Nephi's brothers, so this chapter is drawing on a verse already in the corpus, but for the other half of it: 1 Nephi took the refusal, Jacob takes the definition.

4:6.text: And the Lord said, If ye had faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye might say unto this sycamine tree, Be thou plucked up by the root, and be thou planted in the sea; and it should obey you.

provenance.route: Luke 17:6 (the tree) + Matthew 21:21 / Mark 11:23 (the mountain) + Mark 4:41 / Matthew 8:27 (the sea) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “obey you” — this exact form, not an inflection like “obeyed you” — is a KJV singleton, Luke 17:6, the sycamine tree obeying — a KJV hapax. “and the sea obey” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 4:41 and Matthew 8:27, both of the same stilling. The mountain moved by faith is Matthew 17:20, Matthew 21:21 and Mark 11:23.
provenance.significance: Jacob names three obedient things in one breath — 'the very trees obey us, or the mountains, or the waves of the sea' — and the KJV has exactly one faith-saying for each, in the same order they are conventionally taught: the tree that should obey you (Luke 17:6), the mountain removed and cast into the sea (Matthew 21:21), the wind and the sea that obey him (Mark 4:41). The list is not a general claim about nature; it is a catalogue of the Gospels' three demonstrations, and the verb Jacob uses for all three is the verb Luke uses for the first and Mark for the third.

4:6.note: 'Insomuch that we truly can command in the name of Jesus, and the very trees obey us, or the mountains, or the waves of the sea.' No long run, which is why the machine streams found only the commonplace 'in the name of Jesus' here; the case is that three separate KJV faith-sayings are compressed into one clause with their distinctive nouns intact, and that Jacob's 'obey' is the Gospels' word in two of the three. The transposition is that in the KJV the sea obeys HIM and the tree would obey YOU if you had faith; Jacob claims both for the ministers.

4:8.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

provenance.other: “great and marvellous” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and 15:3, and only 15:3 continues 'are thy works'. The 1830 edition spells the word 'marvellous', which is the KJV's spelling; 1920 modernized it to 'marvelous' and the borrowing is fainter in the modern text than in the first edition (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: This is the same verse 1 Nephi 1:14 used for Lehi's praise, and the argument made there applies again: Revelation 15:3 labels the words it lends as 'the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb'. Across the book boundary the borrowing changes hands — Lehi sang it, Jacob preaches from it — and it changes person with them, 'thy works' becoming 'the works of the Lord'. What Jacob then does with it is new: Revelation's next clause is 'just and true are thy WAYS', and Jacob's next two clauses are about God's ways being unsearchable and no man knowing them. He has taken the couplet and turned its second half into the problem the rest of the paragraph solves.

4:8.note: 'Behold, great and marvellous are the works of the Lord.' Four words in order from one of the two KJV verses that has them, with 'thy works' converted to third person for a sermon rather than a hymn. Adjudicated afresh here rather than by cross-reference because this is a new book and a new voice (ADJUDICATING §4); the first adjudication is at 1 Nephi 1:14, where the same verse is borrowed in the second person as praise.

4:8.text: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!

provenance.other: “how unsearchable” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:33, and “the depth of the riches” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one; “past finding out” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 11:33 and Job 9:10. Jacob 4:8 has the depth, the 'how unsearchable', and the finding out, in Romans's order.
provenance.significance: This is the doorway into the chapter's controlling source. Romans 11:33 is the doxology that closes Paul's argument about Israel's blindness and stumbling, and Jacob 4:8 borrows it six verses before he starts making that argument himself: blindness (4:14), stumbling (4:14-15), the stone (4:15-17), and 'I will unfold this mystery' (4:18), which is Romans 11:25's 'this mystery' about the same blindness. Paul reaches the doxology at the end of Romans 11 and Jacob puts it at the beginning of his own version, so that the whole discourse on the Jews is framed as an instance of what the doxology says: his ways are past finding out. Recovering Romans 11 is what makes 4:8's apparently free-standing piety a thesis statement.

4:8.note: 'How unsearchable are the depths of the mysteries of Him; and it is impossible that man should find out all his ways.' Romans 11:33 reads 'O the depth of the riches … how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out'. Three of its distinctive elements — depth, 'how unsearchable', and the impossibility of finding out his ways — arrive in order, with 'judgments' exchanged for 'mysteries'. The exchange is not neutral: mystery is Romans 11:25's own word for what Paul is about to disclose, and Jacob will use it at 4:18.

4:9.text: Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.

provenance.route: Hebrews 11:3 + Psalm 33:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the worlds were framed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:3; “he spake, and it was” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 33:9 ('For he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast'). Jacob 4:9 reads 'if God, being able to speak, and the world was; and to speak, and man was created'.
provenance.significance: The double construction — speak, and the thing is — is Psalm 33:9's, which the KJV gives as a couplet of speaking and commanding; Jacob keeps the couplet and turns its second half into his argument, 'why not able to COMMAND the earth'. Hebrews 11:3 supplies the doctrine that the agent of creation is the word, which is the premise Jacob needs; and it is the third borrowing from Hebrews 11 in five verses, after 11:17 at 4:5.

4:9.note: 'By the power of his word, man came upon the face of the earth; which earth was created by the power of his word.' No long run: the case is that two KJV singletons stand behind the two halves of the sentence, and that Jacob's inference (God spoke the world into being, therefore he can command it) is Psalm 33:9's own move from speaking to commanding. Recorded at moderate because creation-by-word is common enough in the KJV that no single verse is compelled.

4:10.text: The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.

provenance.other: “over all his works” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 145:9: 'The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.'
provenance.significance: 1 Nephi opened on this verse — 'the tender mercies of the Lord is over all them whom he hath chosen' — and Jacob closes a paragraph on it, and both keep the mercy: Nephi kept the tender mercies and dropped the works, Jacob keeps the works and folds the mercy into a triad, 'in wisdom, and in justice, and in great mercy, over all his works'. The Psalm's claim is that God's mercy has the same extent as his making; Jacob's context is a warning not to counsel the Lord, so the borrowed clause functions as the reason the counsel is unnecessary. Half a verse of Psalm 145 has now framed both ends of the small plates.

4:10.note: A KJV singleton, and the second appearance of Psalm 145:9 in the corpus after 1 Nephi 1:20. Written as a fresh link rather than a cross-reference because Jacob is a different hand and a reader of Jacob shown nothing here would be told there is no borrowing (ADJUDICATING §4); the argument for the source itself was made at 1 Nephi 1:20. Note that the n-gram stream missed the verse there, where the agreement was split across a clause boundary, and found it here, where it is contiguous — the same source, visible or invisible depending on how the borrower phrased it.

4:11.text: Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God.

provenance.route: 2 Corinthians 5:20 + 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 + Philippians 3:10 + Colossians 1:27 + 1 Timothy 3:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Five KJV rarities in one sentence: “be ye reconciled” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 5:20; “the power of the resurrection” occurs in no KJV verse, against Philippians 3:10's 'the power of his resurrection'; “the hope of glory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Colossians 1:27; “good hope” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Thessalonians 2:16; “manifest in the flesh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 3:16. 'Firstfruits' of Christ is 1 Corinthians 15:20-23, the KJV's one use of the term for the risen Christ.
provenance.significance: The verse is a Pauline cento, and the parts have not been chosen at random: reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5), resurrection and firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15), the power of the resurrection (Philippians 3), the hope of glory (Colossians 1), manifestation in the flesh (1 Timothy 3). What Jacob adds is the tense. Paul's firstfruits is Christ already risen; Jacob's readers are to be 'presented as the first fruits of Christ' before he 'manifesteth himself in the flesh', so the whole Pauline vocabulary of accomplished redemption is being used prospectively, by men who date themselves 'many hundred years before his coming' (4:4). That is the chapter's governing conceit, and this verse is where it is densest.

4:11.note: 'Be reconciled unto him, through the atonement of Christ, his only begotten Son, that ye may obtain a resurrection, according to the power of the resurrection which is in Christ, and be presented as the first fruits of Christ, unto God, having faith, and obtained a good hope of glory in him, before he manifesteth himself in the flesh.' Every clause has a KJV home and four of the five phrases are singletons; no single Pauline verse accounts for more than one clause, so 2 Corinthians 5:20 is listed as the source for the governing imperative and the rest as composite. 1830 reads 'first fruits' as two words, which is the KJV's spelling at 1 Corinthians 15:20 ('firstfruits') only in part — the KJV has both forms, and 1920 hyphenated Jacob's. Frederick quotes this verse in full when tracing the Book of Mormon's use of 'Only Begotten Son', and reads it as the most explicit of those uses; he does not propose a source for it.

4:12.text: Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again.

provenance.other: “marvel not that I” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 3:7: 'Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again.' Jacob 4:12 reads 'marvel not that I tell you these things'. The nearest competitors are 1 John 3:13 ('Marvel not, my brethren, if the world hate you') and John 5:28 ('Marvel not at this'), neither of which has the construction.
provenance.significance: Jesus says it to Nicodemus, who has just objected that a man cannot be born a second time; the marvelling being forbidden is a teacher's incredulity at a doctrine that reorders time. Jacob's next clause — 'for why not speak of the atonement of Christ, and attain to a perfect knowledge of him' — asks his readers to accept a knowledge of Christ centuries before Christ, which is the same species of temporal impossibility. The borrowed opening carries its original occasion: an authority told not to be surprised by a chronology he cannot fit.

4:12.note: A KJV singleton and one of the chapter's cleanest borrowings. Note that the verse sits eight verses before John 3:16, whose 'only begotten Son' Jacob has already used twice (4:5, 4:11) — the chapter's contacts with John 3 are with the beginning and the end of one conversation.

4:14.text: For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.

provenance.other: “this mystery” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 11:25 and Colossians 1:27, both of which stand behind this chapter (Colossians 1:27 at 4:11). Romans 11:25 is the KJV's only verse joining a mystery, blindness and Israel; Romans 11:11 supplies 'have they stumbled that they should fall', which is the exact pairing Jacob makes here — 'they must needs fall' because they 'stumble'.
provenance.significance: Jacob's causal chain is Paul's, in Paul's order and with Paul's terms: the Jews are blind, the blindness is judicial (God 'hath taken away his plainness from them', against Romans 11:8's 'God hath given them the spirit of slumber'), it makes them stumble, and the stumbling brings a fall. Paul's word for the whole business is mystery, and Jacob will say 'I will unfold this mystery' four verses later. Where the two differ is the cause: Paul assigns Israel's blindness to God's sovereign arrangement for the Gentiles, and Jacob assigns it to what the Jews wanted — 'because they desired it. And because they desired it, God hath done it' — which is Romans 1:24-28's mechanism imported into Romans 11's argument.

4:14.note: 'Because of their blindness, which blindness came by looking beyond the mark, they must needs fall … God hath done it, that they may stumble.' No long verbal run, and the machine streams proposed nothing at all for this verse; the case is structural — blindness, judicial hardening, stumbling, falling, and a mystery to be disclosed, which is the sequence of Romans 11:7-25 and occurs nowhere else in the KJV as a sequence. 'Looking beyond the mark' is Jacob's own figure and is in no KJV verse; it is the one piece of the chain that is not Paul's.

4:14.text: Wherefore ye be witnesses unto yourselves, that ye are the children of them which killed the prophets.

provenance.route: Matthew 23:31 (or 1 Thessalonians 2:15) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “killed the prophets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 23:31 ('the children of them which killed the prophets'); 1 Thessalonians 2:15 has 'killed the Lord Jesus, and their own prophets'; Matthew 23:37 has 'thou that killest the prophets'. Jacob 4:14 reads 'and killed the Prophets'.
provenance.significance: Both candidates are indictments of a people for the same act, and both are in contexts Jacob is already using: Matthew 23 is the woes on scribes who 'shut up the kingdom of heaven against men', which is Jacob's charge that they 'despised the words of plainness'; 1 Thessalonians 2:15-16 runs on into wrath come upon them 'to the uttermost', which is Jacob's 'they must needs fall'.

4:14.note: A three-word KJV singleton in a verse that is otherwise carried by Romans 11, and one of the two verses that put the whole indictment in one clause. Left at moderate because the phrase is short and because the two candidates cannot be separated on wording — Matthew has the exact form, Paul has the sentiment and the consequence.

4:15.text: Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone;

provenance.route: Romans 9:32-33 (with Isaiah 8:14) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “stumblingstone” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 9:32 and 9:33; “a stone of stumbling” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 8:14 and 1 Peter 2:8. Romans 9:32-33 is the KJV's one place where Israel's stumbling and the stone are a single figure: 'they stumbled at that stumblingstone; as it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence.'
provenance.significance: This is the hinge of the chapter and the reason its two halves belong together. Jacob has just said the Jews stumble (4:14); he now says that 'by the stumbling of the Jews, they will reject the stone upon which they might build'. Only in Romans 9:32-33 does the KJV make the thing stumbled over and the thing rejected the same stone, and it does so by fusing Isaiah 8:14's stone of stumbling with Isaiah 28:16's tried and precious foundation — which is precisely the fusion Jacob then performs across 4:15-17, running from the stumbling to the sure foundation (Isaiah 28:16) to the head of the corner (Psalm 118:22). Jacob is not quoting Romans; he is reproducing Romans's composite stone.

4:15.note: 'By the stumbling of the Jews, they will reject the stone upon which they might build, and have safe foundation.' The verbal contact is thin — stumbling, stone, reject — and the argument is that the combination is not. In the KJV the stone is either a stumblingblock (Isaiah 8:14) or a foundation (Isaiah 28:16) or a rejected head of the corner (Psalm 118:22); it is Romans 9 and 1 Peter 2 that weld the three into one figure, and Jacob has the welded figure. Note that Jacob adds a possibility the New Testament passages do not — the stone is one they MIGHT build on, and 4:17 asks whether they can yet.

4:16.text: Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.

provenance.mt: Isaiah 28:16 — 'a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation'.
provenance.other: “sure foundation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 28:16. The New Testament quotations of Isaiah 28:16 — Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:6 — both drop the phrase: Romans has 'a stumblingstone and rock of offence' and 1 Peter 'a chief corner stone, elect, precious'. So the one distinctive phrase Jacob takes is the one the New Testament does not carry.
provenance.significance: A mediation result in the negative, and it matters because 4:17 will go the other way. Isaiah 28:16 is quoted twice in the New Testament and neither quotation preserves 'sure foundation'; Jacob has it, twice ('the only sure foundation', 4:16; 'the sure foundation', 4:17). So the stone material in this chapter is not taken wholesale from one testament: the foundation comes from the Hebrew prophet in the KJV's Old Testament wording, and the corner, one verse later, comes from the Gospels' wording of the Psalm. Two verses, two directions.

4:16.note: 'This stone shall become the great, and the last, and the only sure foundation, upon which the Jews can build.' 'Sure foundation' is a KJV singleton and Jacob has flagged the borrowing himself — 'according to the Scriptures'. Hardy's appendix gives Isaiah 28:16 here. Note that 'the great, and the last' is not Isaiah's; the KJV's 'first and the last' formula belongs to Isaiah 44:6 and Revelation 1:11, and Jacob has replaced 'first' with 'great', which is the only word in the sentence that is his.

4:17.text: The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.

provenance.mt: Psalm 118:22 — 'The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.'
provenance.route: Psalm 118:22 → Matthew 21:42 / Mark 12:10 / Luke 20:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Psalm 118:22 is quoted five times in the KJV New Testament and the KJV wording differs at two points. (1) The verb: the Psalm has 'refused'; Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10 and Luke 20:17 have 'rejected'; Acts 4:11 has 'set at nought of you builders'; 1 Peter 2:7 has 'disallowed'. (2) The noun: the Psalm has 'the head STONE of the corner'; all five New Testament quotations have 'the head of the corner', with no 'stone'. Jacob 4:15 reads 'they will reject the stone', 4:17 'after having rejected the sure foundation … that it may become the head of their corner'. “the head of their corner” occurs in no KJV verse; “the builders refused” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “the builders rejected” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all Synoptic.
provenance.significance: The chapter's mediation test, and the book of Jacob's first. The Book of Mormon has the New Testament's form at both points where the KJV's Old Testament and New Testament differ — 'rejected', not 'refused'; 'the head of the corner', not 'the head stone of the corner'. And it has the Synoptic form specifically: Acts 4:11 rewords the verb entirely ('set at nought of you builders') and 1 Peter 2:7 gives 'disallowed', so of the five New Testament witnesses only Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10 and Luke 20:17 supply 'rejected'. The result confirms the pattern 1 Nephi established at 2:22, 6:4, 10:8, 15:18 and 22:20, where the borrowed Old Testament text arrives in its New Testament clothes; the recorded counter-examples are 1 Nephi 13:37 and 19:17, both Isaiah 52. Metalepsis does the rest: in all three Synoptics the verse is the punchline of the parable of the wicked husbandmen, spoken by Jesus to the chief priests about themselves, and Matthew's next words are 'the kingdom of God shall be taken from you'. Jacob asks 'how is it possible that these, after having rejected the sure foundation, can ever build upon it' — which is the parable's question, put by a man who says he is prophesying four hundred years before the parable is told.
provenance.alternative: Acts 4:11 and 1 Peter 2:7 are the two New Testament quotations that reword the verb; neither can be the source, since Jacob has 'reject' at 4:15 and 4:17.

4:17.note: 'That it may become the head of their corner.' `mediation-check.py` reports no decisive divergence for this verse, and that verdict is wrong in an instructive way: the tool cannot score an ABSENCE, so it could not see that Jacob lacks the Psalm's 'stone' in 'the head STONE of the corner' exactly as the New Testament quotations lack it. Read by eye, the verse is decided twice over — once by the missing 'stone' and once by 'rejected' against the Psalm's 'refused' — and both times on the New Testament side, and within the New Testament on the Synoptic side. This is the same class of trap ADJUDICATING §4 records for pronouns: the check ignores what is not there. Hardy's appendix gives all five references at this verse without choosing among them; the choice is the finding.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.17 (Psalm 118:22, Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10, Luke 20:17, Acts 4:11)

4:18.text: For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.

provenance.other: “this mystery” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 11:25 and Colossians 1:27. Romans 11:25's mystery is Israel's partial blindness; Colossians 1:27's is 'Christ in you, the hope of glory', which this chapter has already used at 4:11.
provenance.significance: Jacob announces the mystery he is about to unfold and then unfolds it in Jacob 5, the allegory of the olive tree — which is Romans 11:17-24's figure, the natural branches broken off and the wild grafted in. So the chapter's last verse and the next chapter's whole content sit inside the passage that has been supplying its vocabulary since 4:8: Romans 11's doxology opened the discourse, Romans 11's blindness and stumbling carried 4:14, and Romans 11's mystery introduces the olive tree. Paul's own order is doxology last; Jacob has inverted it and put the doxology first.

4:18.whyNot: Two words, both ordinary, and 'unfold this mystery' is not a KJV construction — the KJV's verbs for a mystery are 'make known' and 'be ignorant of'. The link rests almost entirely on the surrounding Romans 11 material at 4:8 and 4:14 and on what Jacob 5 turns out to be; taken alone the verse would not carry it.
4:18.note: 'I will unfold this mystery, unto you.' Recorded as the closing bracket on the chapter's Romans 11 frame rather than as an independent borrowing. The confirmation is in the next chapter: Hardy's appendix gives Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9 and Romans 11:17-24 for the allegory Jacob is here promising, and Romans 11:25 is the verse that stands between Paul's olive tree and his doxology, exactly where Jacob's announcement stands between his own doxology (4:8) and his olive tree.
